english: If there had been an axe within reach, or a poker, or any weapon that could have gashed a hole in his father’s chest and killed him, there and then, James would have grabbed it. Such were the extremes of feeling that Mr. Ramsay stirred in his children just by being there. He stood, as he stood now, lean as a knife, narrow as the blade of one, grinning sarcastically. He was pleased not only to disillusion his son and make fun of his wife, who was ten thousand times better than he was in every way (James thought), but also, secretly, to be vain about how accurate his judgment was. What he said was true. It was always true. He was incapable of untruth. He never tampered with a fact, never softened an unpleasant word to suit the pleasure or convenience of any living being, least of all his own children. They, born of his body, ought to know from childhood that life is difficult; that facts don’t bend; and that the passage to that fabled land where our brightest hopes are put out, where our frail boats go down in darkness (here Mr. Ramsay would straighten his back and narrow his little blue eyes at the horizon), is one that needs, above all, courage, truth, and the power to endure.

Sådanne yderligheder af følelse vakte hr. Ramsay i sine børn blot ved at være til stede. Han stod, som han stod nu, mager som en kniv, smal som dens æg, og grinede sarkastisk. Han fandt ikke blot fornøjelse i at skuffe sin søn og gøre nar af sin hustru, der var ti tusind gange bedre, end han var, på alle måder (mente James), men også i al hemmelighed at være stolt af, hvor nøjagtig hans dømmekraft var. Det, han sagde, var sandt. Det var altid sandt. Han var ude af stand til usandhed. Han rørte aldrig ved en kendsgerning, mildnede aldrig et ubehageligt ord for at tilfredsstille eller lette noget levende væsen, allermindst hans egne børn. De, født af hans legeme, burde fra barndommen vide, at livet er svært; at kendsgerninger ikke bøjer sig; og at overfarten til det sagnomspundne land, hvor vore klareste forhåbninger slukkes, hvor vore spinkle både går under i mørket (her ville hr. english: Strife, divisions, differences of opinion, prejudices twisted into the very fiber of their being—oh, that they should start so early, Mrs. Ramsay lamented. They were so critical, her children. They talked such nonsense. She went out of the dining room, holding James by the hand, since he would not go with the others. It seemed such nonsense to her—inventing differences, when people, heaven knows, were different enough without that. The real differences, she thought, standing by the drawing-room window, are enough, quite enough. What she had in mind at that moment was rich and poor, high and low. The well-born received some respect from her, half grudging, for didn’t she have in her own veins the blood of that very noble, if slightly mythical, Italian house, whose daughters, scattered about English drawing rooms in the nineteenth century, had lisped so charmingly and stormed so wildly? All her wit and her bearing and her temper came from them, and not from the sluggish English or the cold Scots. But more deeply she brooded on the other problem, of rich and poor, and the things she saw with her own eyes, weekly, daily, here or in London. She would visit this widow or that struggling wife in person, with a bag on her arm and a notebook and pencil, and write down wages and spending, employment and unemployment, in columns carefully ruled for the purpose. She hoped that in this way she would stop being a private woman whose charity was half a sop to her own indignation, half a relief to her own curiosity, and would become what, with her untrained mind, she greatly admired: an investigator, shedding light on the social problem.

De velbårne fik en vis respekt af hende, halvt modstræbende, for havde hun ikke i sine egne årer blod fra det højadelige, om end lidt mytiske italienske hus, hvis døtre, spredt rundt i engelske salonger i det nittende århundrede, havde læspet så charmerende og raset så vildt? Al hendes vid og hendes holdning og hendes temperament kom fra dem og ikke fra de trægt engelske eller de kolde skotter. Men dybere grundede hun over det andet problem, rig og fattig, og de ting, hun så med sine egne øjne, ugentlig, daglig, her eller i London. Hun besøgte i egen person denne enke eller hin slidende hustru, med en taske på armen og en notesbog og en blyant, og skrev lønninger og forbrug, beskæftigelse og arbejdsløshed op, i kolonner omhyggeligt optrukket til formålet. english: But here, as she turned the page, her search for the picture of a rake or a mowing machine was suddenly interrupted. There had been a gruff murmur, broken now and then as pipes were taken out and put back in, which had kept assuring her, though she could not hear what was said (sitting as she was in the window), that the men were talking happily. This sound had gone on for half an hour now, and had taken its soothing place in the scale of sounds pressing in on her, such as the tap of balls on bats, and the sharp, sudden bark now and then, “How’s that? How’s that?” of the children playing cricket. And it had stopped. That left only the monotonous fall of the waves on the beach. For the most part the waves beat a measured and soothing rhythm to her thoughts, and seemed to repeat comfortingly over and over, as she sat with the children, the words of some old lullaby, murmured by nature: “I am guarding you—I am your support.” But at other times, suddenly and unexpectedly, especially when her mind lifted itself a little from the task actually in hand, they had no such kind meaning. Instead, like a ghostly roll of drums, they beat out relentlessly the measure of life, made you think of the island being destroyed and swallowed by the sea, and warned her, whose day had slipped past in one quick task after another, that it was all as fleeting as a rainbow. Now this sound of the waves, which had been muffled and hidden under the other sounds, suddenly thundered hollow in her ears and made her look up with a rush of terror.

english: The two of them had rooms in the village, and so, walking in and walking out and parting late on doormats, they had exchanged little remarks about the soup, about the children, about one thing and another, and these had made them allies. So now, when he took up his position beside her in his judicial way (he was old enough to be her father too: a botanist and a widower, who smelled of soap and was very scrupulous and clean), she just stood there. He just stood there. Excellent shoes, he observed of hers. They let the toes spread out naturally. Since they lodged in the same house, he had also noticed how orderly she was—up before breakfast and off to paint, alone, he believed. Presumably she was poor, and she certainly lacked Miss Doyle’s complexion and allure; but she had a good sense which, in his eyes, put her above that young lady. Take now, for instance: when Ramsay came bearing down on them, shouting and waving his arms, Miss Briscoe understood, he felt certain.

english: “It suddenly gets cold. The sun seems to give less heat,” she said, glancing around, for it was still bright enough. The grass kept its soft deep green; purple passionflowers starred the greenery on the house; and from the high blue, rooks let fall their cool cries. But something moved and flashed; a silver wing turned in the air. It was September, after all—mid-September—and it was past six in the evening. So they wandered off down the garden the usual way, by the tennis lawn and the pampas grass, to the gap in the thick hedge. Red-hot pokers guarded it like braziers of clear burning coal, and between them the blue water of the bay looked bluer than ever.

english: They came there regularly every evening, drawn by some need. It was as if the water floated off and set sailing thoughts that had grown stagnant on dry land, and even gave their bodies some kind of physical relief. First the pulse of color flooded the bay with blue, and the heart expanded with it and the body swam, only to be checked and chilled the next instant by the prickly blackness on the ruffled waves. Then, from behind the great black rock, almost every evening, a fountain of white water spurted up at irregular moments, so that you had to watch for it, and it was a delight when it came. And while you waited for that, you watched wave after wave on the pale half-moon of the beach, smoothly shedding a film of mother-of-pearl again and again.

english: The Ramsays weren’t rich, and how they managed it all was a wonder. Eight children! Eight children fed on philosophy! And here came another one, Jasper this time, wandering by to take a shot at a bird, as he put it casually, and pumping Lily’s hand like a pump handle on his way past, so that Mr. Bankes said bitterly how _she_ was a favorite. Now there was schooling to think about (though true, Mrs. Ramsay perhaps had a little money of her own), to say nothing of the everyday wear and tear on the shoes and stockings of those “great fellows,” well-grown, angular, ruthless young things every one of them. As for telling them apart, or knowing the order they came in, he couldn’t. In private he named them after the kings and queens of England: Cam the Wicked, James the Ruthless, Andrew the Just, Prue the Fair—because Prue would be beautiful, he thought, how could she not be?—and Andrew would have brains. Walking up the drive, while Lily Briscoe said yes and no and capped his remarks (she was in love with them all, in love with this world), he weighed up Ramsay’s case. He felt sorry for him; he envied him. It was as though he had watched Ramsay shed all the glories of isolation and austerity that crowned him as a young man, and load himself for good with fluttering wings and clucking domestic life. They gave him something—William Bankes granted that. It would have been nice if Cam had stuck a flower in his buttonhole, or climbed over his shoulder the way she climbed over her father’s, to look at a picture of Vesuvius erupting. But his old friends couldn’t help feeling that they had also destroyed something. What would a stranger make of him now? What did this Lily Briscoe make of him? Who could fail to notice that habits were growing on him—eccentricities, perhaps weaknesses? That a man with his intellect could sink so low—no, the phrase was too harsh—could lean so heavily on other people’s praise: that was astonishing.
danish_before_fix: Familien Ramsay var ikke rig, og hvordan de klarede det hele, var et under. Otte børn! Otte børn fodret med filosofi! Og her kom endnu et, Jasper denne gang, der slentrede forbi for at skyde efter en fugl, som han sagde henkastet, og pumpede Lilys hånd som en pumpeswingel på vej forbi, så hr. Bankes bittert sagde, at _hun_ var en favorit. Nu var der skolegang at tænke på (selv om fru Ramsay sandt at sige måske havde lidt penge af sig selv), for ikke at tale om det daglige slid på sko og strømper på de »store fyre«, velvoksne, kantede, hensynsløse unge væsener hver eneste af dem. At skelne dem fra hinanden eller kende rækkefølgen, de kom i, kunne han ikke. I det stille opkaldte han dem efter Englands konger og dronninger: Cam den Onde, James den Hensynsløse, Andrew den Retfærdige, Prue den Skønne — for Prue ville blive smuk, mente han, hvordan kunne hun andet? — og Andrew ville få hjerne. Mens han gik op ad indkørslen, og Lily Briscoe sagde ja og nej og tog hans bemærkninger op (hun var forelsket i dem alle, forelsket i denne verden), afvejede han Ramsays sag. Han ynkede ham; han misundte ham. Det var, som om han havde set Ramsay lægge al den ensomheds og strenghedens glans fra sig, som kronede ham som ung, og for stedse læsse sig til med flagrende vinger og kluksende husliv. De gav ham noget — det indrømmede William Bankes. Det ville have været rart, hvis Cam havde stukket en blomst i hans knaphul eller var kravlet over hans skulder, som hun kravlede over sin fars, for at se på et billede af Vesuvs udbrud. Men hans gamle venner kunne ikke lade være med at føle, at de også havde ødelagt noget. Hvad ville en fremmed tænke om ham nu? Hvad tænkte denne Lily Briscoe om ham? Hvem kunne undgå at lægge mærke til, at vaner var ved at tage overhånd hos ham — særheder, måske svagheder? At en mand med hans intellekt kunne synke så lavt — nej, udtrykket var for hårdt — kunne læne sig så tungt op ad andres ros: det var forbløffende.

english: So whenever Mr. Ramsay’s work came to mind, what she saw was a scrubbed kitchen table. Just now it sat lodged in the fork of a pear tree, since they had come into the orchard. With a painful effort she concentrated her mind—not on the tree’s silver-studded bark, nor on its leaves shaped like fish, but on a phantom kitchen table stuck up there with its four legs in the air: one of those scrubbed plank tables, grained and knotted, whose virtue seems to have been laid bare by years of muscular honesty. Naturally, if you spent your days seeing angular essences like this, shrinking lovely evenings, with all their flamingo clouds and their blue and silver, down to a four-legged table of white pine (and the finest minds did exactly that), naturally you could not be judged like other people.
danish_before_fix: Så hver gang hr. Ramsays arbejde faldt hende ind, var det, hun så, et skrubbet køkkenbord. Lige nu sad det fastklemt i en gren af et pæretræ, siden de var kommet ind i frugthaven. Med en smertefuld anstrengelse samlede hun tankerne — ikke om træets sølvbeslåede bark eller dets fiskeformede blade, men om et fantombord, der sad fast deroppe med fire ben i vejret: et af de skrubbede plankebord, åreforede og knastede, hvis dyd synes at være blevet blottet af års muskuløs ærlighed. Naturligvis, hvis man tilbragte sine dage med at se kantede essenser som denne, med at skrumpe dejlige aftener med alle deres flamingoskyer og deres blå og sølv ned til et firbenet bord af hvidt fyr (og de fineste hjerner gjorde netop det), kunne man naturligvis ikke bedømmes som andre mennesker.

english: “My dear, stand still,” she said. For James, in his jealousy, did not like serving as a measuring block for the Lighthouse keeper’s little boy, and he fidgeted on purpose; and if he did that, how could she see whether it was too long or too short? she asked.
danish_before_fix: »Kære, stå stille,« sagde hun. For James, i sin jalousi, brød sig ikke om at tjene som målestok for Fyrvogterens lille dreng, og han sprællede med vilje; og hvis han gjorde det, hvordan kunne hun så se, om den var for lang eller for kort? spurgte hun.

english: She glanced up—what demon had got into him, her youngest, her darling?—and her eye fell on the room and on the chairs, and she thought how dreadfully shabby they were. Their guts, as Andrew put it the other day, were spilling all over the floor. But then, she asked herself, why buy good chairs only to have them ruined up here all winter, when the house, with just one old woman to look after it, was absolutely dripping with damp? Never mind. The rent came to exactly twopence halfpenny; the children adored the place; it was good for her husband to be three thousand miles—or, to be accurate, three hundred—away from his library and his lectures and his disciples; and there was space for guests. Mats, camp beds, crazy ghosts of chairs and tables that had finished their years of service in London—up here they did well enough; and so did a photograph or two, and books. Books, she thought, seemed to grow on their own. She never had time to read them. Alas! Even the ones given to her and inscribed by the poet in his own hand—“For her whose wishes must be obeyed” … “The happier Helen of our days” …—it was a disgrace, but she had never read them. And neither Croom on the Mind nor Bates on the Savage Customs of Polynesia (“My dear, stand still,” she said) was something you could send to the Lighthouse. Sooner or later, she supposed, the house would be so shabby that something would have to be done about it. If only they could learn to wipe their feet and stop bringing the beach indoors—that would be something. As for crabs, she had to admit, if Andrew really wanted to dissect them, or if Jasper thought seaweed could be made into soup, there was no stopping it; nor Rose’s collections—shells, reeds, stones; for her children were gifted, though each in a quite different way. And so, she sighed, her eyes taking in the whole room from floor to ceiling while she held the stocking to James’s leg, the result was that things grew shabbier and shabbier, summer after summer. The mat was fading; the wallpaper was coming loose and flapping. Nobody could tell anymore that the pattern was roses. Still, things are bound to spoil if every door in a house stands open all the time and not one locksmith in all Scotland can fix a bolt. What good did it do to drape a green cashmere shawl over the corner of a picture frame? Within two weeks it would be the color of pea soup. But the doors were what annoyed her; every single door was left open. She listened. The drawing-room door stood open; so did the hall door; the bedroom doors sounded open too; and the landing window was certainly open, since she had opened it herself. Windows open, doors shut—simple as that was, could none of them remember it? At night she would go into the maids’ bedrooms and find them shut up tight as ovens—all except Marie’s, the Swiss girl, who would sooner do without a bath than without fresh air. But then at home, the girl had said, “the mountains are so beautiful.” She had said it last night, gazing out of the window with tears in her eyes. “The mountains are so beautiful.” Her father was dying there, as Mrs. Ramsay knew. He was going to leave them fatherless. When the girl spoke, all Mrs. Ramsay’s scolding and demonstrating (how to make a bed, how to open a window, her hands closing and spreading like a Frenchwoman’s) had quietly folded itself around her, just as a bird’s wings fold themselves quietly after a flight through the sunshine, and the blue of its feathers turns from bright steel to soft purple. She had stood there without a word, because there was nothing to say. He had cancer of the throat. Remembering it—how she had stood there, how the girl had said, “At home the mountains are so beautiful,” and how there was no hope, no hope of any kind—she felt a spasm of irritation, and spoke sharply to James:
danish_before_fix: Hun så op — hvilken dæmon var faret i ham, hendes yngste, hendes skat? — og hendes blik faldt på stuen og på stolene, og hun tænkte, hvor forfærdeligt slidte de var. Deres indvolde, som Andrew havde sagt forleden, væltede ud over gulvet. Men så spurgte hun sig selv, hvorfor købe gode stole bare for at få dem ødelagt heroppe hele vinteren, når huset, med blot én gammel kone til at passe det, var helt drivende af fugt? Lad det nu være. Lejen kom til nøjagtig to og en halv penny; børnene elskede stedet; det var godt for hendes mand at være tre tusind mil — eller, for at være nøjagtig, tre hundrede — fra sit bibliotek og sine forelæsninger og sine disciple; og der var plads til gæster. Måtter, feltsenge, skøre spøgelser af stole og borde, der havde udtjent deres tid i London — heroppe gjorde de fyldest; og det gjorde et fotografi eller to, og bøger også. Bøger, tænkte hun, syntes at vokse af sig selv. Hun havde aldrig tid til at læse dem. Ak! Selv dem, hun havde fået og som digteren havde skrevet i med egen hånd — »Til hende, hvis ønsker må adlydes« … »Vor tids lykkeligere Helena« … — det var en skam, men hun havde aldrig læst dem. Og hverken Croom om Sindet eller Bates om Polynesiens vilde skikke (»Kære, stå stille,« sagde hun) var noget, man kunne sende til Fyret. Før eller siden, mente hun, ville huset blive så slidt, at der måtte gøres noget ved det. Hvis de bare kunne lære at tørre fødderne og holde op med at slæbe stranden ind i huset — det ville være noget. Hvad krabberne angik, måtte hun indrømme, at hvis Andrew virkelig ville dissekere dem, eller hvis Jasper mente, at tang kunne laves til suppe, var der ingen vej udenom; og heller ikke om Roses samlinger — muslingeskaller, siv, sten; for hendes børn var begavede, om end hver på en helt forskellig måde. Og sådan, sukkede hun, mens hendes øjne tog hele stuen ind fra gulv til loft, og hun holdt strømpen op mod Jamess ben, blev resultatet, at tingene blev slidtere og slidtere, sommer efter sommer. Måtten blegnede; tapetet løsnede sig og flagrede. Ingen kunne mere se, at mønstret var roser. Alligevel er ting nødt til at forgå, hvis hver eneste dør i et hus står åben hele tiden, og ikke en eneste låsesmed i hele Skotland kan reparere en slå. Hvad nyttede det at hænge et grønt kashmirsjal over hjørnet af en billedramme? Inden for to uger ville det have farve som ærtesuppe. Men det var dørene, der irriterede hende; hver eneste dør blev stående åben. Hun lyttede. Dagligstuedøren stod åben; det gjorde entredøren også; soveværelsesdørene lød også åbne; og vinduet på reposen var bestemt åbent, for hun havde selv åbnet det. Vinduer åbne, døre lukkede — så enkelt som det var, kunne ingen af dem huske det? Om natten gik hun ind på pigernes soveværelser og fandt dem lukket tæt som ovne — alle undtagen Maries, den schweiziske piges, der hellere ville undvære et bad end frisk luft. Men hjemme, havde pigen sagt, »er bjergene så smukke«. Hun havde sagt det i går aftes, mens hun så ud af vinduet med tårer i øjnene. »Bjergene er så smukke.« Hendes far lå for døden dér, som fru Ramsay vidste. Han ville efterlade dem uden far. Da pigen talte, var al fru Ramsays skænden og demonstrerende (hvordan man redte en seng, hvordan man åbnede et vindue, hendes hænder lukkende og spredende sig som en franskkvindes) stille foldet sig sammen om hende, ligesom en fugls vinger stille folder sig sammen efter en flugt gennem solskinnet, og blåt på dens fjer skifter fra lys stål til blød lilla. Hun havde stået der uden et ord, fordi der intet var at sige. Han havde kræft i halsen. Da hun huskede det — hvordan hun havde stået der, hvordan pigen havde sagt: »Hjemme er bjergene så smukke,« og hvordan der ikke var noget håb, ikke noget håb af nogen art — følte hun et anfald af irritation og talte skarpt til James:

english: “But she’s no more aware of her beauty than a child is,” said Mr. Bankes, putting down the receiver and crossing the room to see how the workmen were getting on with a hotel they were building at the back of his house. And he thought of Mrs. Ramsay as he watched that bustle among the unfinished walls. For there was always, he thought, something incongruous to be worked into the harmony of her face. She would clap a deerstalker’s hat on her head; she would run across the lawn in galoshes to snatch a child out of mischief. So if it was merely her beauty you thought of, you had to remember the quivering thing, the living thing (they were carrying bricks up a little plank as he watched them), and work it into the picture. Or if you thought of her simply as a woman, you had to give her some freak of idiosyncrasy; or imagine some hidden wish to throw off her royalty of form, as if her beauty bored her, and everything men say about beauty, and she wanted only to be like other people, insignificant. He did not know. He did not know. He must get to his work.)
danish_before_fix: »Men hun er ikke mere bevidst om sin skønhed end et barn,« sagde hr. Bankes, lagde røret på og gik over stuen for at se, hvordan arbejderne klarede sig med et hotel, de byggede bag hans hus. Og han tænkte på fru Ramsay, mens han så på det myreflittige liv blandt de uafsluttede mure. For der var altid, mente han, noget misforholdsmæssigt, der skulle arbejdes ind i harmonien i hendes ansigt. Hun kunne finde på at klaske en jagthat på hovedet; hun kunne finde på at løbe over plænen i galoscher for at hente et barn ud af fortræd. Så hvis det kun var hendes skønhed, man tænkte på, måtte man huske den dirrende ting, den levende ting (de bar mursten op ad en lille planke, mens han så på dem), og arbejde den ind i billedet. Eller hvis man tænkte på hende blot som kvinde, måtte man give hende en eller anden fiks idé; eller forestille sig et eller andet skjult ønske om at kaste sin formens kongelighed af sig, som om hendes skønhed keder hende, og alt det, mænd siger om skønhed, og hun kun ville være som andre mennesker, ubetydelig. Han vidste det ikke. Han vidste det ikke. Han måtte i gang med sit arbejde.)

english: Starting out of her musing, she gave meaning to words she had been holding in her mind, meaningless, for a long stretch of time. “Someone had blundered”—the line from Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade.” She fixed her shortsighted eyes on her husband, who was now bearing down on her, and gazed steadily until, as he came close, she could see (the jingle paired itself off in her head) that something had happened; someone had blundered. But she could not for the life of her think what.
danish_before_fix: Hun for sammen af sin dagdrøm og gav mening til ord, som hun i lang tid havde båret rundt på i sit sind uden at de betød noget. »Nogen havde fejlet« — linjen fra Tennysons »Lette kavaleris angreb«. Hun rettede sine nærsynede øjne mod sin mand, der nu kom stormende hen imod hende, og så stift på ham, indtil hun, da han kom tæt på, kunne se (remsen parrede sig selv op i hendes hoved), at der var sket noget; nogen havde fejlet. Men hun kunne ikke i verden begribe hvad.

english: Not for the world would she have spoken to him. She knew the signs: his eyes turned away, and a curious gathering-in of his whole person, as if he were wrapping himself up and needed privacy in which to get his balance back. They told her he was outraged and in anguish. She stroked James’s head; she passed on to him what she felt for her husband. As she watched him color the white dress shirt of a gentleman in the Army and Navy Stores catalogue yellow with his chalk, she thought what a delight it would be to her if he turned out to be a great artist; and why shouldn’t he? He had a splendid forehead. Then, looking up as her husband passed her once more, she was relieved to find that the ruin was veiled. Domestic life had won; habit was crooning its soothing rhythm. So when he stopped deliberately at the window as his turn came round again, and bent down, teasing and whimsical, to tickle James’s bare calf with a sprig of something, she scolded him lightly for having sent off “that poor young man,” Charles Tansley. Tansley had had to go in and write his dissertation, he said.
danish_before_fix: Hun ville ikke for alt i verden have talt til ham. Hun kendte tegnene: hans øjne, der vendte sig bort, og en sælsom sammentrækning af hele hans person, som om han svøbte sig ind og trængte til ro for at få balancen tilbage. De fortalte hende, at han var oprørt og pint. Hun strøg James over hovedet; hun gav videre til ham, hvad hun følte for sin mand. Mens hun så ham farve en herreskjorte i Army and Navy Stores-kataloget gul med sin kridt, tænkte hun på, hvilken fryd det ville være for hende, hvis han blev en stor kunstner; og hvorfor skulle han ikke det? Han havde en pragtfuld pande. Så, da hun så op, idet hendes mand gik forbi hende endnu en gang, kunne hun med lettelse se, at ruinen var tilsløret. Hjemmelivet havde sejret; vanen nynnede sin beroligende rytme. Så da han bevidst standsede ved vinduet, da turen kom rundt igen, og bøjede sig ned, drillende og lunefuld, for at kildre Jamess bare lægge med en kvist af et eller andet, skændte hun let på ham, fordi han havde sendt »den stakkels unge mand«, Charles Tansley, væk. Tansley havde måttet gå ind og skrive på sin afhandling, sagde han.

english: She was perfectly willing to take his word for it, she said. It only meant they wouldn’t need to cut sandwiches—nothing more. Being a woman, she naturally had people coming to her all day long with one thing or another; this one wanted this, that one wanted that; the children were growing up; she often felt she was nothing but a sponge, soaked through with human emotions. And then he said, Damn you. He said, It must rain. He said, It won’t rain; and at once a Heaven of safety opened in front of her. There was no one she revered more. She wasn’t good enough to tie his shoelaces, she felt.
danish_before_fix: Hun var fuldt og helt villig til at tage hans ord for gode varer, sagde hun. Det betød bare, at de ikke skulle smøre sandwich — ikke andet. Som kvinde havde hun naturligvis folk kommende til sig hele dagen med det ene og det andet; den ville have det, og den anden ville have det; børnene voksede op; hun følte ofte, at hun ikke var andet end en svamp, gennemvædet af menneskelige følelser. Og så sagde han, Fanden tage dig. Han sagde, Det må regne. Han sagde, Det kommer ikke til at regne; og straks åbnede en himmel af tryghed sig foran hende. Der var ingen, hun nærede større ærefrygt for. Hun var ikke god nok til at binde hans snørebånd, syntes hun.

english: “Someone had blundered,” he said again, striding off, up and down the terrace.
danish_before_fix: »Nogen havde fejlet,« sagde han igen, mens han strøg af sted, op og ned ad terrassen.
danish_after_fix: »Nogen havde begået en fejl,« sagde han igen, mens han strøg af sted, op og ned ad terrassen.

english: How extraordinarily his tone had changed, though! It was like the cuckoo—“in June he gets out of tune”—as though he were trying out, groping toward, some phrase to suit a new mood, and, with nothing but this one to hand, made do with it, cracked as it was. Yet it sounded absurd, “Someone had blundered,” spoken that way, almost like a question, with no conviction at all, in a singsong voice. Mrs. Ramsay couldn’t help smiling, and before long, sure enough, pacing up and down, he hummed it, let it go, and went quiet.
danish_before_fix: Hvor ekstraordinært hans tonefald dog havde ændret sig! Det var som gøgen — »i juni slår han fejl i tonen« — som om han prøvede sig frem, famlede efter en frase, der passede til et nyt stemningsleje, og, da han ikke havde andet ved hånden end denne ene, klarede sig med den, revnet som den var. Alligevel lød det absurd, »Nogen havde fejlet«, sagt på den måde, næsten som et spørgsmål, helt uden overbevisning, i en messende tone. Fru Ramsay kunne ikke lade være med at smile, og lidt efter, så sandelig, mens han travede op og ned, nynnede han det, lod det falde og blev stille.

english: Then came to his aid the qualities that would have saved a ship’s crew adrift on a scorching sea with a flask of water and six biscuits—endurance and fairness, foresight, devotion, skill. Well then, R is—what is R?
danish_before_fix: Så kom de egenskaber ham til hjælp, der ville have reddet et skibs mandskab, drivende på et brændende hav med en flaske vand og seks skibskiks — udholdenhed og retfærdighed, forudseenhed, hengivenhed, færdighed. Nå, så er R — hvad er R?
